derivations.claim: Fix $x\in B$, put $e=x-x_*$, and write $E=r(x)-r(x_*)-J(x)e$. By [F1] and [A1], $r(x)=J(x)e+E$ with $\|E\|_2\le(L/2)\|e\|_2^2$.

Let $p$ be the exact Gauss-Newton step and set $h:=p+e$. For every $v\in\mathbb R^n$, minimality of $p$ gives $\frac12\|r(x)+J(x)(p+tv)\|_2^2\ge\frac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2$ for all real $t$. Expanding in $t$ shows the linear coefficient $v^TJ(x)^T(r(x)+J(x)p)$ must be zero (otherwise a sufficiently small $t$ of the opposite sign decreases the quadratic). Since this holds for every $v$, $J(x)^T(J(x)h+E)=0$ by step 1.1.

Set $q:=-h$. Step 2.1 gives $J(x)^T(E-J(x)q)=0$, so $E-J(x)q$ is orthogonal to $J(x)q$; hence $\|E\|_2^2=\|J(x)q\|_2^2+\|E-J(x)q\|_2^2\ge\|J(x)q\|_2^2$. By [A2], $\|J(x)q\|_2\ge\sigma\|q\|_2$. Therefore $\|x+p-x_*\|_2=\|h\|_2=\|q\|_2\le\|E\|_2/\sigma\le C\|e\|_2^2$.

If $C=0$, step 3.1 gives $x_1=x_*$. If $C>0$ and $\|x_0-x_*\|_2\le1/(2C)$, step 3.1 gives $\|x_1-x_*\|_2\le\frac12\|x_0-x_*\|_2$, so $x_1\in B$; induction repeats the same bound for every $k$, and $\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le2^{-k}\|x_0-x_*\|_2\to0$.

This algorithm performs one finite-budget LM trial update. Inputs are $x\in U$, a residual function $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$, its Jacobian $J(x)$, a fixed nonsingular $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), a floor $\lambda_{\min}>0$, current damping $\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$, factors $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, a trust radius $\Delta>0$, and an attempt cap $N\ge1$. A computed run may include a certificate that the exact scalar product $J(x)^Tr(x)$ is zero. Put $\phi(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2/2$ and $m_0(p)=\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2/2$. In exact mode the step is the unique minimizer of
$$\tfrac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|Dp\|_2^2,$$
which is equivalent to solving
$$(J(x)^TJ(x)+\lambda D^TD)p=-J(x)^Tr(x).$$
In computed mode the returned vector is only a candidate for this same subproblem; no exact minimizer claim is made.


For attempts $j=1,\ldots,N$, do the following with the current damping. After a damping change, construct a new augmented matrix and obtain a report for that actual matrix; do not reuse an earlier damping value's factorization or report.

1. In exact arithmetic, if $J(x)^Tr(x)=0$, return stationary before calling the linear solver. In a computed run, return stationary before the solve only with the supplied certificate that this exact gradient is zero; if computing $J(x)^Tr(x)$ fails, return gradient-evaluation-failure; if the computed product is a rounded zero without that certificate, return gradient-unverified and do not form a ratio. Otherwise perform the augmented construction and linear solve afresh inside this attempt at its current damping: Form $A_\lambda=[J(x);\sqrt\lambda D]$ and $s_\lambda=[r(x);0]$, then call [[alg-gauss-newton-qr-svd-step-with-rank-safeguard]] in QR mode on $(A_\lambda,s_\lambda)$. Exact mode uses the exact positive square root and requires a supplied exact reduced factorization of $A_\lambda$ for each call; absence of that factorization returns linear-solve-failure. This matrix has full column rank because $D$ is nonsingular and $\lambda>0$. In computed mode, copy the stored $J(x)$ and $r(x)$ into the top blocks, compute $t=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)$, then fill the bottom block entries $\operatorname{fl}(tD_{ij})$ in increasing row and column order and fill the appended residual entries with exact zeros. Any first arithmetic or range failure in this construction returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. The call receives a computed QR report for this actual stored $A_\lambda$. A computed-candidate is usable only when that report includes the low-level procedure's independently verified full-rank certificate $s_\lambda>0$ for the actual stored matrix, namely $\|A_\lambda v\|_2\ge s_\lambda\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Pass this bound as the computed report's certificate field; it is not inferred from a nonzero computed diagonal or from positive definiteness of the ideal exact system alone. A rank-unverified report and every other status besides exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode are unusable and return linear-solve-failure with the report. A computed-candidate remains a candidate and carries no convergence guarantee. If the solver status is not exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode, return linear-solve-failure with its report; in particular, rank-unverified is a failure, not a usable trial.
2. If exact mode returns $p=0$ after the nonzero-gradient check, return linear-solve-failure with the inconsistent exact solve report. If computed mode returns $p=0$, return zero-step-unverified and do not compute a ratio. For every remaining candidate $p$ (the zero candidates have already returned a status), compute $\operatorname{pred}=m_0(0)-m_0(p)$. If this computation fails, return model-evaluation-failure; if $\operatorname{pred}\le0$, return nonpositive-predicted-decrease. In either case do not compute a ratio.
3. If computing $x+p$ or $Dp$ fails in the selected arithmetic, return trial-evaluation-failure. If $x+p\notin U$ or $\|Dp\|_2>\Delta$, reject the trial and compute the damping update $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$ and continue.
4. Otherwise evaluate $r(x+p)$ and compute $\operatorname{ared}=\phi(x)-\phi(x+p)$ and $\rho=\operatorname{ared}/\operatorname{pred}$. A failed trial evaluation or nonfinite computed result returns trial-evaluation-failure. If $\rho<\eta_1$, reject and compute $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that damping update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$. If this was attempt $N$, return rejection-budget-exhausted; otherwise continue.
5. If $\rho\ge\eta_1$, first determine the next damping. If also $\rho\ge\eta_2$ and $\|Dp\|_2=\Delta$, compute $q=\lambda/\gamma$ in exact mode and $q=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda/\gamma)$ in computed mode. If this division fails, has a nonfinite or nonpositive result, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report, without accepting that trial. Otherwise set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\max\{\lambda_{\min},q\}$. In every other accepted case set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\lambda$. Only after the next damping is available, accept and return $x+p$, $p$, $\rho$, and $\lambda_{\rm next}$.

If all $N$ attempts are rejected, return rejection-budget-exhausted. The equality in the boundary test is exact for exact arithmetic and is the equality test on stored values in a computed run. No claim is made that every finite budget succeeds.

$D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be nonsingular, let $\lambda>0$, and put
$g:=J^Tr$. Assume $g\ne0$. There is a unique $p_\lambda$ satisfying
$$\bigl(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD\bigr)p_\lambda=-g.$$

$\Delta_\lambda:=\|z_\lambda\|_2>0$. Then $z_\lambda$ uniquely minimizes
$$q_\lambda(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2$$
over $\mathbb R^n$, and globally minimizes the unregularized model
$$m(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2$$

[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]]. Its predicted reduction is
positive and, in the original step coordinates,
$$m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2>0.$$

$\|J(y)-J(z)\|_2\le L\|y-z\|_2$ for all $y,z\in K$, where the matrix norm is

$$\|r(x)-r(x_*)-J(x)(x-x_*)\|_2\le\tfrac L2\|x-x_*\|_2^2.$$

induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has

inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.

   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$

   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of

$r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be of class $C^2$ (each component
has continuous partial derivatives through order two, as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Define
$$\phi(x):=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2,$$
and let $J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be the Jacobian with $i$th row
$\nabla r_i(x)^T$. Then $\phi$ is of class $C^2$ and
$$\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^T r(x),\qquad \nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x).$$

when $r(x)=0$, but need not vanish at a nonzero-residual stationary point.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$

   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

citations.quote:
This algorithm performs one finite-budget LM trial update. Inputs are $x\in U$, a residual function $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$, its Jacobian $J(x)$, a fixed nonsingular $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), a floor $\lambda_{\min}>0$, current damping $\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$, factors $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, a trust radius $\Delta>0$, and an attempt cap $N\ge1$. A computed run may include a certificate that the exact scalar product $J(x)^Tr(x)$ is zero. Put $\phi(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2/2$ and $m_0(p)=\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2/2$. In exact mode the step is the unique minimizer of
$$\tfrac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|Dp\|_2^2,$$
which is equivalent to solving
$$(J(x)^TJ(x)+\lambda D^TD)p=-J(x)^Tr(x).$$
In computed mode the returned vector is only a candidate for this same subproblem; no exact minimizer claim is made.


For attempts $j=1,\ldots,N$, do the following with the current damping. After a damping change, construct a new augmented matrix and obtain a report for that actual matrix; do not reuse an earlier damping value's factorization or report.

1. In exact arithmetic, if $J(x)^Tr(x)=0$, return stationary before calling the linear solver. In a computed run, return stationary before the solve only with the supplied certificate that this exact gradient is zero; if computing $J(x)^Tr(x)$ fails, return gradient-evaluation-failure; if the computed product is a rounded zero without that certificate, return gradient-unverified and do not form a ratio. Otherwise perform the augmented construction and linear solve afresh inside this attempt at its current damping: Form $A_\lambda=[J(x);\sqrt\lambda D]$ and $s_\lambda=[r(x);0]$, then call [[alg-gauss-newton-qr-svd-step-with-rank-safeguard]] in QR mode on $(A_\lambda,s_\lambda)$. Exact mode uses the exact positive square root and requires a supplied exact reduced factorization of $A_\lambda$ for each call; absence of that factorization returns linear-solve-failure. This matrix has full column rank because $D$ is nonsingular and $\lambda>0$. In computed mode, copy the stored $J(x)$ and $r(x)$ into the top blocks, compute $t=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)$, then fill the bottom block entries $\operatorname{fl}(tD_{ij})$ in increasing row and column order and fill the appended residual entries with exact zeros. Any first arithmetic or range failure in this construction returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. The call receives a computed QR report for this actual stored $A_\lambda$. A computed-candidate is usable only when that report includes the low-level procedure's independently verified full-rank certificate $s_\lambda>0$ for the actual stored matrix, namely $\|A_\lambda v\|_2\ge s_\lambda\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Pass this bound as the computed report's certificate field; it is not inferred from a nonzero computed diagonal or from positive definiteness of the ideal exact system alone. A rank-unverified report and every other status besides exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode are unusable and return linear-solve-failure with the report. A computed-candidate remains a candidate and carries no convergence guarantee. If the solver status is not exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode, return linear-solve-failure with its report; in particular, rank-unverified is a failure, not a usable trial.
2. If exact mode returns $p=0$ after the nonzero-gradient check, return linear-solve-failure with the inconsistent exact solve report. If computed mode returns $p=0$, return zero-step-unverified and do not compute a ratio. For every remaining candidate $p$ (the zero candidates have already returned a status), compute $\operatorname{pred}=m_0(0)-m_0(p)$. If this computation fails, return model-evaluation-failure; if $\operatorname{pred}\le0$, return nonpositive-predicted-decrease. In either case do not compute a ratio.
3. If computing $x+p$ or $Dp$ fails in the selected arithmetic, return trial-evaluation-failure. If $x+p\notin U$ or $\|Dp\|_2>\Delta$, reject the trial and compute the damping update $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$ and continue.
4. Otherwise evaluate $r(x+p)$ and compute $\operatorname{ared}=\phi(x)-\phi(x+p)$ and $\rho=\operatorname{ared}/\operatorname{pred}$. A failed trial evaluation or nonfinite computed result returns trial-evaluation-failure. If $\rho<\eta_1$, reject and compute $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that damping update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$. If this was attempt $N$, return rejection-budget-exhausted; otherwise continue.
5. If $\rho\ge\eta_1$, first determine the next damping. If also $\rho\ge\eta_2$ and $\|Dp\|_2=\Delta$, compute $q=\lambda/\gamma$ in exact mode and $q=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda/\gamma)$ in computed mode. If this division fails, has a nonfinite or nonpositive result, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report, without accepting that trial. Otherwise set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\max\{\lambda_{\min},q\}$. In every other accepted case set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\lambda$. Only after the next damping is available, accept and return $x+p$, $p$, $\rho$, and $\lambda_{\rm next}$.

If all $N$ attempts are rejected, return rejection-budget-exhausted. The equality in the boundary test is exact for exact arithmetic and is the equality test on stored values in a computed run. No claim is made that every finite budget succeeds.

Let $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let
$J=Dr$, and let $\phi=\|r\|_2^2/2$. Fix $x_0\in U$ and suppose its sublevel set
$S=\{x\in U:\phi(x)\le\phi(x_0)\}$ is compact. Put
$S_1=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\operatorname{dist}(y,S)\le1\}$ and assume $S_1\subseteq U$.
On $S_1$, suppose $\|r(x)\|_2\le R_0$, $\|J(x)\|_2\le M$, and $J$ is
$L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean induced matrix norm.
Fix nonsingular $D$, numbers $d,d_+>0$ with
$\|Dv\|_2\ge d\|v\|_2$ and
$\max\{\|D\|_2,\|D^T\|_2\}\le d_+$, and parameters
$\lambda_{\min}>0$, $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, and $\Delta>0$.
Define
$$C_D:=d_+^2+M^2/\lambda_{\min},\quad C_E:=\tfrac L2(R_0+M)+\tfrac{L^2}{8},\quad P:=\min\{1,\Delta/(2d_+)\},$$
$$\Lambda:=\max\left\{\lambda_{\min},\frac{MR_0}{d^2P},\frac{C_EC_D^2}{(1-\eta_2)d^6}\right\},\quad N:=1+\left\lceil\frac{\log(\Lambda/\lambda_{\min})}{\log\gamma}\right\rceil.$$
At any $x\in S$ with $g:=\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^Tr(x)\ne0$, an exact LM trial with damping
$\lambda\ge\Lambda$ has $0<\operatorname{pred}$, $\|Dp_\lambda\|_2\le\Delta/2$,
and $\rho\ge\eta_2$. Therefore, if the algorithm starts an iteration with
$\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$ and has at least $N$ trials, it either accepts an
earlier trial with $\rho\ge\eta_1$ or accepts by the $N$th trial. This conclusion
assumes exact subproblem solves and exact objective evaluations.

Let $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $r\in\mathbb R^m$, $m,n\ge1$, let
$D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be nonsingular, let $\lambda>0$, and put
$g:=J^Tr$. Assume $g\ne0$. There is a unique $p_\lambda$ satisfying
$$\bigl(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD\bigr)p_\lambda=-g.$$
Set $z_\lambda:=Dp_\lambda$, $\widetilde J:=JD^{-1}$, and
$\Delta_\lambda:=\|z_\lambda\|_2>0$. Then $z_\lambda$ uniquely minimizes
$$q_\lambda(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2$$
over $\mathbb R^n$, and globally minimizes the unregularized model
$$m(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2$$
over the trust-region ball $\|z\|_2\le\Delta_\lambda$ of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]]. Its predicted reduction is
positive and, in the original step coordinates,
$$m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2>0.$$

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let
$r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be of class $C^2$ (each component
has continuous partial derivatives through order two, as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Define
$$\phi(x):=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2,$$
and let $J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be the Jacobian with $i$th row
$\nabla r_i(x)^T$. Then $\phi$ is of class $C^2$ and
$$\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^T r(x),\qquad \nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x).$$

The second term in the Hessian is the residual-curvature term. It vanishes
when $r(x)=0$, but need not vanish at a nonzero-residual stationary point.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

derivations.claim: At a nonstationary $x_k\in S$, [F2] shows that the iteration either accepts an earlier trial or accepts once $\lambda\ge\Lambda$, within $N$ attempts. Thus no rejection-budget status occurs. The accepted actual reduction is $\rho\,\operatorname{pred}\ge\eta_1\operatorname{pred}>0$ by [F1], so $\phi(x_{k+1})<\phi(x_k)\le\phi(x_0)$ and $x_{k+1}\in S$. Induction keeps all iterates in $S$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let
$r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be of class $C^2$ (each component
has continuous partial derivatives through order two, as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Define
$$\phi(x):=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2,$$
and let $J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be the Jacobian with $i$th row
$\nabla r_i(x)^T$. Then $\phi$ is of class $C^2$ and
$$\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^T r(x),\qquad \nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x).$$

The second term in the Hessian is the residual-curvature term. It vanishes
when $r(x)=0$, but need not vanish at a nonzero-residual stationary point.

Input a stored residual $r\in\mathbb R^m$, a stored Jacobian $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$ (using the convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a factorization mode QR or SVD, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), and a declared singular-value threshold $\tau\ge0$. A computed QR report may also carry a verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ asserting $\|Jv\|_2\ge s\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. The target exact step, when it is returned, is the unique minimizer of $\frac12\|r+Jp\|_2^2$ and hence solves $J^TJp=-J^Tr$; this target is asserted only on a full-column-rank branch. Do not form $J^TJ$ in either solve path.

For QR mode the exact and computed routes are disjoint. Exact mode requires a supplied exact reduced factorization $J=QR$ with $Q^TQ=I_n$; only this exact factorization may reach the exact-step branch. Computed mode consumes a computed QR report or forms one by setting $C=[J\mid-r]$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,n$, applying [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] to the active part of column $k$ and all trailing columns of $C$, including its last right-hand-side column. Propagate the first factorization failure. After a successful computed loop, the report consists of the computed upper-triangular block $\widehat R$ and the first $n$ entries $\widehat y$ of the transformed last column. These rounded outputs are not an exact factorization of $J$ and cannot be supplied to the exact branch. In exact mode, a zero diagonal in $R$ returns rank-deficient; otherwise solve $Rp=Q^T(-r)$ by backward substitution and return exact-step($p$). In computed mode, a zero diagonal returns rank-deficient-candidate. Otherwise initialize storage for $\widehat p_0,\ldots,\widehat p_{n-1}$ with all components unassigned, then for $i=n-1,n-2,\ldots,0$ compute $s_i$ by setting $s_i=0$ and, for $j=i+1,i+2,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order, updating $s_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(s_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat R_{ij}\widehat p_j))$; then compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat y_i-s_i)$ and $\widehat p_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/\widehat R_{ii})$. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. A nonzero computed diagonal without an independently verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ for the input matrix $J$ returns rank-unverified with the computed candidate but no full-rank claim. With that certificate, return computed-candidate($\widehat p$). A nonzero computed diagonal alone is not a full-rank certificate. The computed-QR backward-stability conclusion of [[thm-computed-full-rank-least-squares-backward-stability]] is attached only when all of that theorem's successful-execution, arithmetic, and nonsingularity hypotheses are supplied; otherwise no backward-stability conclusion is returned.

For SVD mode, the input includes an exact factorization $J=U\Sigma V^T$, or a computed report containing finite stored factors $\widehat U_1$, $\widehat\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_i)$ with nonnegative entries, and $\widehat V$, together with certified intervals $[\ell_i,u_i]$ satisfying $\ell_i\le\sigma_i(J)\le u_i$ for each of the $n$ singular values relevant to full column rank. In the exact case, if any $\sigma_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold and no Gauss-Newton step. If every $\sigma_i>\tau$, return
$$p=-V\,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_n^{-1})\,U_1^Tr,$$
where $U_1$ consists of the corresponding $n$ left singular vectors. For a computed report, if any $u_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold; if any interval satisfies $\ell_i\le\tau<u_i$, return rank-unverified; if every lower endpoint exceeds $\tau$ but some stored $\widehat\sigma_i=0$, return factorization-failure; otherwise return the finite candidate
$$\widehat p=-\widehat V\,\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^{-1})\,\widehat U_1^Tr$$
with status computed-candidate and make no accuracy claim beyond the supplied report. The certified intervals determine only the threshold branch; no computed-SVD accuracy bound is asserted. A computed SVD routine is not defined here; the SVD branch consumes its report.

If $m<n$, return unsupported-shape; if the selected factorization reports failure, return factorization-failure; every status other than exact-step is explicitly not a certified exact full-rank Gauss-Newton step.

Let $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^2$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let
$\phi=\|r\|_2^2/2$, $J=Dr$, $A=J^TJ$, and
$S(x)=\sum_i r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)$. Let $x_*\in U$ satisfy
$J(x_*)^Tr(x_*)=0$, and let the closed ball
$B=\{x:\|x-x_*\|_2\le R\}$ lie in $U$, with $R>0$. Suppose on $B$:

- $J(x)$ has full column rank and smallest singular value at least $\sigma>0$;
- $\|J(x)\|_2\le M$;
- $J$ is $L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean induced matrix norm;
- $\|S(x)\|_2\le\kappa$.

Define $q=(\kappa+MLR)/\sigma^2$ and assume $q<1$. For the exact full-rank
Gauss-Newton step $p(x)=-A(x)^{-1}J(x)^Tr(x)$, every $x\in B$ satisfies
$$\|x+p(x)-x_*\|_2\le q\|x-x_*\|_2.$$
Consequently the exact iterates from any $x_0\in B$ stay in $B$ and converge
to $x_*$ at a linear rate no larger than $q$. The curvature hypothesis
controls the residual term $S$; no quadratic rate is claimed when it is
nonzero.

derivations.claim: Here $J(x)=(1,x)^T$, so $J(x)^TJ(x)=1+x^2>0$ for every $x$. Also $J(x)^Tr(x)=x+\frac12x+\frac12x^3=\frac32x+\frac12x^3$, which vanishes at $x_*=0$ while $r(0)=(0,1/2)^T$ has norm $1/2$.

The scalar normal equation is $(1+x^2)p=-\frac32x-\frac12x^3$, so $p=-x(3+x^2)/(2(1+x^2))$. Adding $x$ gives $x_+=x(x^2-1)/(2(1+x^2))$. For $0<|x|<1$, $|x_+|/|x|=(1-x^2)/(2(1+x^2))<1/2$, so every such iterate stays in the interval and converges to zero.

On $B=[-1/10,1/10]$, both $\|J(x)\|_2$ and $\|J(x)^T\|_2$ are at most $11/10$, both are $1$-Lipschitz, and $\|J(x)v\|_2\ge|v|$; also $S(x)=1/2+x^2/2\le101/200$. Thus the local contraction theorem [F3] applies with $R=1/10$, $M=11/10$, $L=1$, $\sigma=1$, $\kappa=101/200$, and $q=123/200<1$.

As $x\to0$ through nonzero values, $|x_+|/|x|\to1/2$, whereas $|x_+|/|x|^2=(1-x^2)/(2|x|(1+x^2))\to+\infty$. No finite quadratic error constant can therefore hold near the stationary point. This exact example shows that the linear rate in [F3] cannot generally be strengthened when the residual is nonzero.
